Beth Nelson whipped into the driveway kicking up all the rocks the road had to give. Michael Stone could see the cloud of dust following her car from the time she hit the long sandy road. The kind of road native Floridians know all too well. Sugar sand. Washboard. pulled into the Stone family driveway at the end of a long sandy road. The kind that Floridians know well. Sugar sand. Michael's English bulldog, Chesty looked up at him and gave a slight whine. Michael felt the same way. He had known Beth since they were in kindergarten and he had always found her irritating. Even back then, when they were under the tutelage of Miss Hargrove, who for forty years had been everybody’s kindergarten teacher in Hilltop, Beth had sought attention and gotten it. In a town like Hilltop, if you went looking for attention, you got it. It was the type of place where everybody knew everybody else, and minding your own business was a foreign concept. Michael had grown up itching to get out of the place, but after his stint in the Marine Corps, he had settled right back down in his hometown, and planned to grow old there. Sure, everybody knew everybody’s business, but the inquisitiveness of one’s neighbor was mostly out of a desire to be there when help was needed. However, there would always be a few busybodies in a town like Hilltop.
Beth got out of her car and waved across the yard frantically to Michael who stood up from his position at the well pump. Even though Michael had known Beth for more than three decades, she was really more Charlotte’s friend than his. Her thick mascara had run down her cheeks, and she was talking fast.
Drama accompanied Beth, and that drama was usually about her ex-husband Jerry and how he was a deadbeat dad to her three kids. Michael had mentioned to Charlotte on more than one occasion that he was afraid that her constant bad-mouthing would poison Charlotte’s mind against all men, but Charlotte had just laughed him off. Quite the contrary, she had said, all that talk about Jerry had made her thank God every night that she had gotten herself a man like Michael. Besides, Beth needed some positivity in her life, and Charlotte could give her that. Michael had let it drop, because even Charlotte had her limits. There was only so much Beth Nelson a person could take. 
"Hey Beth,” said Michael from across the yard, "I’ll go let Charlotte know you’re here. She’s just getting the kids started on their school work.”
"No, Mike, wait. I’m here to see you. Do you have a minute?”
He had lots of minutes. His Marine recruiter had made it seem like lucrative job offers would be thrown at his feet after he served his four years. But since moving back to Hilltop the work had been sparse. He had taken every odd job he could find. And the tourist season would be drawing to a close after the blueberry festival ended that weekend. Nobody in the town was offering a job that would support a wife and four kids. 
Commuting to the city was out of the question. Spend two-thirds of his life away from his wife and family for a few more bucks? No thanks. The last thing he needed though, was for Beth to know they were hurting for money. She’d have that juicy little tidbit spread all over town in a heartbeat.
But Beth looked desperate, so he put on a cordial face.
"Well, my schedule is pretty full today, but I've got a couple of minutes. What's up?” God please don’t let this be about man trouble, he added mentally. He and Charlotte had been happily married for 9 years. Not that it had been a cakewalk, but he just couldn’t relate to all the he-said she-said back and forth that Beth was always going on about. Michael always wondered why people put themselves in situations like this. Don't they think about their actions beforehand? And why don't they realize it before it's too late and get out of whatever they're mixed up in?
"Have you heard about Jerry?” she asked, her voice cracking.
"What’s he done now?” He knew it had to be about Jerry.
"He went and got himself killed,” she choked up, and then broke down completely.
"Char,” Michael called toward the house, desperately hoping she would hear him. He turned back to Beth. 
"Killed?” Michael asked. "How?”
Beth wiped her nose with a tissue then continued, "They found his body last night in his carriage, slumped down on the footboard.”
"Do they know who did it?”
"They think it was me!” she wailed. 
Charlotte came out of the house and crossed the yard. Michael caught her up while Beth tried to control her sobbing. Two minutes later Charlotte had guided Beth into the living room with a box of tissues and told Michael to put on some coffee. When he returned with the mugs, Beth was still sniffling, but had calmed down considerably. Charlotte had that way about her.
"I couldn't remember about cream and sugar, Beth," said Michael. "So here is whatever you need." He placed a pile of sweetener and sugar packets, left over from something that he couldn't remember, and some Walmart half and half. His preferred coffee was black because it's easy to get black coffee anywhere that serves coffee.
"Now Beth, you let us know whatever you need us to do. Okay? We’re both here for you. Isn’t that right, Mike?” she said as she looked up at Michael, making it clear he was to answer in the affirmative.
"Yeah, sure. Of course,” said Michael as he sat down. "That’s what friends are for.” Using the term 'friends' lightly. 
Beth turned to Michael and said, "I’m glad you feel that way, Mike. Because the reason I came out here is that I was hoping you could help by looking into this for me. See if you can figure out who did this to Jerry. I know it’s not your job, but you’re the only person I know who might be able to help.”
"Oh, Beth, I meant that I could cut your grass or something like that. I mean, I’d like to help you, but I’m not a cop or anything. I’m sure Sheriff Jones will take care of it.”
"But they’ve got it out for me.”
"Who?” asked Michael.
"Sheriff Jones and Deputy Earl!” 
"What makes you think that?” asked Charlotte. But before Beth could answer, the baby monitor screeched and Charlotte excused herself, promising to return soon. 
Michael looked down at his coffee cup, hoping the baby monitor was enough of a distraction to change the subject away from him investigating a death. He had no experience in anything like that. Plus he had income problems and couldn't spend a bunch of time on a pointless mission to try to find out what happened to Frank who probably keeled over from drinking too much.
"Mike, you’ve gotta help me. I’m serious.”
"Have they questioned you?”
"Not officially. I think the sheriff was afraid of looking bad, picking on the widow, you know. It’s an election year.”
Michael thought it interesting how yesterday Beth was just Jerry’s ex-wife and now she was referring to herself as ‘the widow.’ Always like Beth to manipulate a situation.
"Well Beth, he’s running uncontested, just like he has for the past thirty years.”
"But Marge called me a few minutes ago, and she told me I’m their prime suspect.”
Marge Smith was Deputy Earl’s second cousin. He had gotten her the job as the receptionist for the sheriff’s office. It was a plum position for Marge, who happened to love good gossip. Every bit of it in Hilltop passed through the sheriff's office even if it didn't have anything to do with the law. In the previous month Marge had single handedly and somewhat anonymously disseminated messages about DUI arrests, burnt meals cooked by new brides, and elective surgeries of Hilltop residents. There was some sort of secretary underground where all of these bits of information were passed. 
"Oh come on, she was probably exaggerating. You know how she likes to stir the pot,” he said. 
"No, I think they’re really out to get me.”
"They’re not that bad. They’re just small town cops. Look, the sheriff’s probably watched more crime shows than anybody I know. He’s got that kit of detective supplies he carries around with him in the trunk of his car.”
"He’s just itching to solve a big crime,” said Beth, "And now he’s going to try to pin this on me.”
"Just give him a break, Beth. Maybe he's getting a little carried away. It’s not his fault nothing big ever happens in this town. I'm sure that whatever he said, Marge just took it the wrong way."
"Look, DCF called this morning, saying they were gonna do a welfare check this evening. They said it’s standard, Mike, but I don’t buy it. I think Sheriff Jones put them up to it. And they’re just looking for an excuse to take the kids. It was bad enough when they started coming after Jerry got that DUI.” 
"That was five years ago,” said Michael. 
"Yeah, but I haven’t forgotten the look in that woman’s eyes. She was looking for any excuse to take the boys away from me. I don’t know what I would do without my kids, Mike.”
Just then Ethan came running down the stairs. Michael’s eight-year-old was the spitting image of him. "Hey Beth! Hey Dad, can we go fishing today?” 
Chesty’s ears perked up and he lifted his gaze to Michael. Even though he was an English bulldog he loved to go fishing. He couldn't swim too well and didn't try anymore since the time Charlotte put him in a doggy life jacket. She was afraid he was going to go over face forward under water because of his shape. He hangs out on the shore now barking at turtles and birds and whatever else may cross his path.
"We’ll see.”
"Please, Dad?”
"I said we’ll see.”
"But when you say we’ll see that means no.”
"It’s not a for sure no, but it will be if you don’t go back upstairs and get back on your school work.” Chesty plopped his wrinkled head back on the ground. He knew what 'we'll see' meant too.
"Yes, sir!” said Ethan as he gave a salute and then shot back upstairs.
"How would you feel if they came over here and tried to take away Ethan?” Beth asked, her eyes pleading.
"I wouldn’t let them get through the door,” he admitted.
"I really need your help, Mike. And I can pay you.”
Now Michael's ears perked up like Chesty's. This was a change. Beth was usually asking for money, not giving it. Jerry was perpetually behind on child-support and alimony. She caught his look and held up her hands.
"Look, I know, I usually don’t have extra cash. But right now I do.”
"But Beth, I’m not a cop.”
"But you were in the military.”
"Well, yeah. But that’s different.”
"You’re good at figuring stuff out, Mike. You always have been. Remember back in fifth grade when somebody kept stealing my lunch? You caught Corbin Baumgartner red-handed."
"We were kids, Beth, and plus, it was obvious. Your mom put your name on the sandwich bag, and he was dumb enough to leave it in his unzipped backpack."
"Well nobody else figured it out. Come on, please? I don’t know who else to turn to. And look, Charlotte told me about the tax lien.”
Michael’s face grew hot. "We don’t need any money. Just go cooperate with Sheriff Jones. I’m sure you have nothing to worry about.” 
Beth glared at him. "Fine! I just hope for my kids’ sakes, their daddy’s murder doesn’t go unsolved and they have to grow up wondering if they’re next. I swear, Mike, if they take my kids away from me, I’ll never forgive you.” She stormed out the door and marched to her car.
"What did you say to her?” Charlotte asked as she came down the stairs. Without waiting for a reply she handed the baby off to Michael and flew out the door. 
Michael walked out on the porch and watched as the two women talked briefly. Beth was pointing an accusing finger at him. Chesty sat next to his feet, softly grumbling.
"I’m right there with you, boy.”
Charlotte continued to talk to her, and then Beth handed her an envelope and sped out of the driveway.  
"She said she can pay more when you’ve cleared her name,” said Charlotte as she pushed the envelope into his hand, took the baby from him, and went inside.
Michael looked down into the envelope. Twenty crisp one hundred dollar bills stared back up at him.

"The property taxes are due whether you like it or not, Mike,” said Charlotte as she loaded the dishwasher. "We’re running out of time. They’re going to take our home right from under us.” She continued loading dishes and waited for a response. They had bought the house two years before with cash that Charlotte had inherited from her grandmother, but the old farmhouse had turned out to be a real money pit. Despite the problems, it was their dream home: five acres they could call their own with plenty of room for the kids to play. Last month they got a notice of back taxes due. 
When Michael didn’t say anything she turned around and asked, "Earth to Mike. Did you hear me?”
He was sitting at the island bar running his finger around the rim of his glass of sweet tea. "Yeah, I heard you. I was just thinking.”
"Well, do you think you could acknowledge me when I say something so I don’t feel like I’m talking into thin air?”
"They can't take our house. We never got the notices in the mail.”
"Mike, they don’t care. They’ve made it clear that it was our responsibility to pay them, even if we didn’t get the notices. I feel like such an idiot for not realizing it.”
"It was my fault. I should have been on top of things. I’m sorry, Char, I’ll figure out what to do.”
"What’s to figure out, Mike?” 
Michael looked at the envelope on the counter next to him. "I’m not taking that money.”
"Give me one good reason why not.”
"Because it’s Beth.”
"And?”
"Come on, Charlotte. You know how she is.”
"She’s not that bad, Mike.”
"We don’t want to get wrapped up in all her drama.” Here Chesty let out two quick yips. "See, Chesty agrees with me.”
"Well, Mike, like her or not, I don’t think we have a choice. We’ve got to get that money together.”
Presently, their four-year-old daughter came into the kitchen and tugged on Michael’s pant leg and said, "Daddy?”
Michael reached down and picked her up onto his lap. "What’s up, Harper?”
"Who’s taking our house?”
Michael looked at Charlotte with a look that said kids really do hear everything. "Nobody, Sugarbug.” He rubbed the top of her head. "Now, you go ask Ethan if he’ll take you outside so you guys can collect the eggs from the nests before it gets too hot out.” He set her down and she ran into the other room. A moment later, Michael heard the backdoor close.
"Nothing is turning out like I thought it would. I thought we’d move back here, settle down, and it’d be easy to get work. And now here I am working odd jobs like some teenage kid.”
Charlotte tilted her head. "Ah, it’s not that bad, Mike.”
"No, it literally is. I gave Mrs. Kelso a quote to clean out her gutters and she told me Hale Anderson’s boy Jason would do it for half that.” 
Charlotte laughed as she put the detergent in and pushed start.
"It’s not funny, Char. Maybe we would have been better off if I would have just stayed in. I mean, I’d be a staff sergeant by now, and-”
Charlotte cut him off, "And, you’d be off in some other country doing God knows what. And you’d miss so much of the kids’ growing up. They need you to be here.” She paused, then said, "And so do I.”
Michael rubbed his face and looked down at the money again. 
	"I just hate the idea of working for Beth.”
"Would you rather be bidding jobs against Jason Anderson?”
"I don’t even know where to start. I’ve never done anything like this before.”
Charlotte came over and put her arms around him. "You’ll figure it out. You always do. Who knows? Maybe if you go over to the Sheriff’s office, they might help you out. And if you go right now, you’ll catch them on their coffee break.” 
"Are you sure she’s innocent?” he asked, raising an eyebrow.
Charlotte swatted him on the shoulder. "Mike!”
"Well, I've heard her tell him to drop dead on more than one occasion.”
"Oh come on, Mike. You know she didn’t mean that. People say that kind of stuff all the time.”
"I believe her exact words were, ‘I hope you drink yourself to death, you good for nothing piece of trash.’”
"Well, he was eight months behind on child support. Beth’s innocent. Now, shoo! Go see if you can find anything out from our good old boys in blue.”
Against his better judgment, Michael loaded up Chesty in the beat up blue Ford pickup and headed for downtown to see what he could find out.

Sheriff Jones and Deputy Carl were sitting around a large wooden desk that was too big for the room. The jailhouse had been built 108 years earlier and was remodeled only twice in its lifetime. At present the motif was circa 1960 and that suited the sheriff just fine seeing that it brought back memories of his childhood. Portraits of past sheriffs and big case news clippings hung on the walls. 
Earl Parker was not, as some suspected, Sheriff Jones’ distant relation. He was merely a local kid who went to the police academy with only the best of intentions and somehow made it through. The sheriff brought him on because he needed a deputy and nobody else who lived in the town wanted the job.
They slurped their thick store brand coffee from stained mugs while they discussed the case that was the talk of the town and even the county. It had been less than 18 hours since Jerry’s body was found and it seemed that everyone had questions for the Sheriff. Even though only a few had had the chance to speak with him, many of them purported to know the details of the case.
Michael arrived outside the office door at the same time as Kevin and Linda Brockton, owners of KLB Realty. The husband and wife were a power couple, and had sold Michael on the farmhouse. 
"The house is looking great,” said Kevin as he held the door open for Michael and Linda.
Linda flashed Michael the well-known smile that was plastered all over every billboard, bench, and shopping cart in town. "You guys got a heck of a deal. Five acres and close to town. I bet with how the market’s doing now, it’s worth triple what you paid for it.”
"Maybe,” said Michael. 
"Good morning, gentlemen,” said Kevin to the sheriff and Earl.
"Morning,” they said in unison.
Sheriff Jones looked expectantly at the threesome. 
"Well, Mike, you were here first,” said Linda.
"No, that’s okay, I can wait,” he said, taking a seat next to the door and hoping he might overhear something useful.
"I heard we had some excitement in town last night,” said Kevin. 
"Jerry Nelson, dead. Who would have thunk it?” said Earl, shaking his head as he stared into his cup of coffee.
Sheriff Jones rolled his eyes. "If anybody was going to an early grave in this town, I would have put my money on Jerry. I think most people would’ve.”
Everyone nodded their heads at this. 
"I’m actually glad you two came in,” said the sheriff. "The town’s up in arms about the blueberry festival. Half of them want to go on with it, the other half say we should cancel it. Since you guys are the big sponsors, celebrating 10 years of your business and all, I told people I’d get your opinion.”
Ah, the master politician, thought Michael. 
"As much as we will all mourn the loss of Jerry, Linda and I have discussed it, and we both think the town should move forward with the festival. A whole bunch of folks need the money it brings in. And you know, you can’t afford to have Hilltop’s business owners mad at you this year.” 
Sheriff Jones drank from his cup then wiped his full mustache with his hand and nodded his head. "Plus, Jennie’s already got the kitchen full of pie plates and flour and whatever. It looks like a factory in there. We even had to eat in the living room last night because the table was covered with pie boxes.” He paused to take another drink. "When the town council asks me, I’m gonna recommend we move forward as scheduled.”
Kevin and Linda exchanged a few more pleasantries, and then left. 
"I think that’s the right move,” said Michael, standing up from his chair. 
"Oh, hey Mike, I had forgotten you were there,” said Sheriff Jones with an awkward smile. "Thanks for stopping by. But, I checked with Jennie, and she said we don’t need any pressure washing done at the moment. I’ll be sure to spread the word that you’re available, though.”
Michael felt his face turning red with embarrassment, but he quickly recovered. "Oh, I didn’t come about that.”
Sheriff Jones cast a glance at Earl, who only raised his eyebrows in answer. The clock on the wall ticked loudly as Michael tried to think of something else to say.
"Is there something we can do for you, Michael?” asked Earl.
"Well, Beth was over at the house this morning and she was really upset.”
Both the sheriff and Earl perked up at this. "Upset? About what time was this?” Earl asked, picking up his pad and pen.
"Oh come on, guys, you can’t be serious. This is Beth Nelson we’re talking about. Earl, she played tee ball with your big brother. Come on.”
Earl leaned forward and lowered his voice. "It’s always who you least suspect, but especially if that person is also the ex-wife. Has she done or said anything suspicious?” 
"Did you see her last night at all?” asked the Sheriff.
Michael looked to them both in disbelief. "No wonder she was so upset. I thought she was exaggerating. But you two really are out to get her.”
Sheriff Jones held his hands up. "Now, now, Michael. Don’t go getting your dander up. It’s our job to investigate this stuff.”
"Well, are you investigating anybody else?” 
Earl laughed. "Oh sure! We’ve got Frank and-”
Sheriff Jones stood up and put a hand on Earl’s shoulder to stop him. "Sorry Michael, that’s need-to-know. Don’t worry about Beth. As long as she didn’t do anything wrong she has nothing to worry about. But you’ll have to excuse us now, we’ve got an investigation to attend to.”
Michael nodded and turned to go. He needed to find Frank Stevens.

"Look Mike, I don’t know anything about what happened last night,” said Frank as he brushed the withers of his horse. 
"You nervous about something, Frank?”
"Of course I  am. Somebody’s going around knocking off carriage drivers.” 
Michael raised his eyebrows. "Were you working last night?”
"You know I work every night.”
"Well did you see anything out of the ordinary?”
Frank cast his eyes up to the barn ceiling and thought for a moment. "Nope. The evening started off pretty busy. Bunch of people here for the blueberry festival. But a storm blew in, so I cut out early and went home.”
"Did you see Jerry’s carriage yesterday?”
Frank frowned. "Of course I did. We see each other all the time. We’re the only two carriage drivers in Hilltop.”
"When did you last see Jerry?” 
Anger flashed in Frank’s eyes. "What, are you the cops or something? It’s none of your business. I don’t have to answer you.”
Chesty let out a low growl. 
Michael bent down and rubbed the dog’s neck to sooth him. "I’m sorry, Frank. I wasn’t trying to accuse you of anything. You see, I’m just trying to help Beth out. Sheriff Jones and Carl are being a little overzealous, and she’s feeling a bit jumpy.”
"Sounds to me like she’s acting guilty. Doesn’t surprise me at all.”
"What makes you say that?”
"One, you and me both know the woman’s got a temper. Two, Jerry was a bum and never paid up like he was supposed to. Three, and here’s the most serious one, I saw them having a real knock-down drag out right in the middle of the street not an hour before they found his body.”
This gave Michael pause. But Charlotte had tossed the idea of Beth being guilty out as ridiculous, and she had a knack for knowing what kind of person someone really was, deep down. With Beth she must have had to really plumb the depths. 
"Is that all you wanted?” said Frank, interrupting his thoughts.
"You didn’t harbor any resentment towards him, Jerry?”
"No.”
"Even though he stole Gatsby from you?”
Frank’s face darkened. "He didn’t steal him. Anyway, that was almost a year ago.”
"Yeah, but everybody knows Jerry cheated you out of him. Got you drunk as a skunk and then beat you at a lousy game of poker. He got your gorgeous Friesian, and you got this half-lame nag with a swayback.
"Hey, don’t talk about Petunia like that,” he said, petting her defensively. "And besides, my business isn’t hurting at all because of my horse. I’m actually having the best year I’ve ever had. Jerry is the one who was struggling. He was lazy. He was only taking half the fares I was getting.” Frank grabbed his ledger book from under his carriage seat and flipped through the last several pages showing Michael the log of paying customers he had. "See, my nights have been full. Business is good. I certainly didn’t have any beef with Jerry that was worth killing him for. If anything, I should have thanked him. Petunia does the same amount of work as Gatsby and she eats almost half as much food. And she’s sweeter, too.” Petunia knickered softly at his praise.
"How long have you been keeping a book like that?”
While Frank slid the book back under the seat. "I’ve been using a ledger since I started. It’s common practice.”
"What all do you keep record of?” asked Michael.
"Just the names of riders, the route and how much the fare was,” said Frank, irritated. "Look, I’ve got stuff to take care of. It’s one of my busiest weekends and now I’m the only carriage in town, so I don’t have time to talk anymore about this.”
Frank mounted his carriage. 
"One more thing, Frank. What time did you say you went home?
"I didn’t,” he said sulkily.
"Well, come on, could you tell me what time you went home? I’m just trying to put together a timeline to help out Beth. And look, I’m mainly thinking of her kids, Frank. She’s a handful, but she is a good mom.”
Frank sighed. "I left at about 6:30, got home at a quarter til.” Michael watched him ride away and thought about all Frank had said.
Michael walked a few blocks up and over and popped back in the sheriff’s office and found Earl alone.
"What are you doing back here, Mike?” asked Earl.
"Hey, Earl, I was just wondering if Jerry had a ledger or something that kept track of his customers.”
"I can’t talk about the investigation with you,” said Earl as he turned away and pretended to work on something.
"Oh, sorry if that was unclear. I’m not asking about your investigation,” said Michael. "It’s just that Jerry was really far behind on child support and he claimed it was because business was slow. But just now I got to wondering if he was lying about that. You know, if he did have some cash stashed away, it’d really help Beth out, being a widow now and all.”
Earl hesitated, "Well, yeah he had a ledger but there was nothing in it to speak of. It seemed normal.”
"Where is it?" asked Michael.
"It's in the evidence locker with all the other evidence."
"Like what?"
"Like evidence, that's like what," said Earl, beginning to get agitated.
"Can I take a look at the ledger?”
"No, it’s evidence.”
"Come on, you just said there was nothing to speak of in it.”
"Sorry, Mike. I’m going to have to ask you to leave.”
Michael had thought of starting an argument with Earl over the ledger, but thought differently of it once he realized that now that he knew there was a ledger he could definitely find some answers. He didn't want Earl to think he really cared so much about getting the ledger because he figured that would cause Earl to talk to the sheriff about it or to simply go to more effort to secure it.

Kimmy had just started her shift at The Cozy Cup when Michael walked in. 
"Afternoon, Mr. Stone,” she said. "Can I get you a cup?” She waved a mug in the air.
"When you call me that, I turn around to look for my dad.”
"Well, I call him Father George, not Mr. Stone.”
"Thanks, but no,” said Michael. "I can’t have caffeine after three. Char says it gets my leg to shaking in the bed and then she can’t sleep. You got a minute?”
"Sure,” said Kimmy. "Let me just go give table two a top off.”
While she was taking care of the elderly couple, Mike went to the window and looked down at the intersection of Maple and Third, where Jerry’s body had been found.
Kimmy sidled up next to him and knelt down to give Chesty a small to-go cup of whipped cream. She gave him a scratch behind the ears as he lapped up the cream, grunting loudly. "Don’t they ever feed you, boy?”
"Only five times a day,” said Michael. He’d never seen a dog that could eat so much.
Kimmy grinned as she stood up. "I asked Nancy about the flyers. She said that you could put one up on the door. But if it gets wet, be sure to replace it with a fresh one. It’s a pet peeve of hers.”
Mike ran his fingers through his hair. He had forgotten about asking to put up his handyman flyers around town. "Ah, actually, that’s not what I’m here about. But thanks, I’ll bring one by later.”  Should I just cross through handyman and put private investigator instead? he wondered. He was pushing forty and still hadn’t figured out what he was going to do with his life. Charlotte always reassured him that he’d find it someday. It was the only thing he had ever doubted her on. 
"I was wondering if you knew anything about what happened last night, Kimmy,” said Michael. "Anybody acting strange or did you see anybody you didn’t recognize?”
"Well, I always see people I don’t recognize,” said Kimmy, slightly confused. Then her eyes lit up. "Hey! Are you investigating or something? Like a private eye?” Mike felt the room get quieter and curious eyes of patrons shift over to them. 
"Shh!” he said, figuring that the fewer people who knew he was investigating, the better. "Look, I’m just doing a favor for Beth, okay?”
"So cool. Can I help?” she asked in a low voice, her eyes eager.
"Did you see anybody acting weird?”
Kimmy tilted her head up in thought. "Uh, no I don’t think so. But once we get busy I don’t really pay much attention to anything except for serving coffee and stuff. The people who found Jerry in the carriage came in here to use the phone to call the sheriff’s office though, because their phone didn’t have any service.”
"How’d they act?” asked Michael.
"Pretty shaken up.”
"Could you see the carriage from here?”
"Oh yeah,” said Kimmy, "it was just right up the street there in front of the barber shop, but it was raining and that street light is still burned out, so I couldn’t really tell much about anything. I told the mayor about the light again yesterday, but I guess he’s got other stuff to deal with. I wish they’d fix it though, because that’s the way I walk home.”
"Did you see anybody on the street or anything out of the ordinary?”
"No. After the couple said they found a body, everybody was crowded around the window, trying to see what was going on, so it’s possible I missed something. Dang it, I wish I would’ve paid closer attention.”
"That’s okay. How about before the couple came in? Did you see anybody up there by the carriage?”
Kimmy chewed her lip. "No, I  mean, like I said, we were really slammed that night.”
"Did you happen to notice when Jerry’s carriage pulled up there?”
She furrowed her brow, and then she slapped the counter, causing the customers to look at them again. Kimmy’s face went pink and she gave Mike an apologetic smile. She went to the payment station and quickly ran through the menus until she found what she was looking for.
